content: In September 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) reclassified intrathoracic lymph node tuberculosis (TB) in children as a form of pulmonary TB. This decision followed an expert consultation and reflects the evolving understanding of TB in pediatric populations. The GRADE system (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) is a framework used to assess the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations in clinical and public health practices. It provides a transparent and systematic approach to decision-making. Settings with high TB transmission are characterized by a significant presence of individuals with undiagnosed or untreated TB, increasing the risk of disease spread. People with TB are most infectious when they are untreated or inadequately treated. Aerosol-generating procedures and the presence of highly susceptible individuals further amplify the risk of transmission. A household contact is defined as someone who has shared the same living space with a person diagnosed with TB (the index case) for one or more nights or for extended periods during the three months preceding the start of treatment. The index case refers to the first identified individual with TB in a specific setting, such as a household, and serves as the focal point for contact investigations. However, the index case is not necessarily the source of the infection. Inpatient healthcare settings are facilities where individuals are admitted and assigned a bed for at least one overnight stay while undergoing diagnosis, treatment, and care. Integrated treatment decision algorithms are tools that use evidence-based scoring of microbiological, clinical, and radiological features to guide clinicians in initiating TB treatment in children. The interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is a blood test that detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection by measuring the immune response to TB bacteria. Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) is caused by strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis that are resistant to at least rifampicin and isoniazid, two key first-line TB drugs. A new case refers to a person newly diagnosed with TB who has never been treated for the disease or has taken TB medications for less than one month. Non-severe pulmonary TB in children, for the purpose of determining treatment duration, includes intrathoracic lymph node TB without airway obstruction, uncomplicated TB pleural effusion, or non-cavitary disease confined to one lung lobe without a miliary pattern. The number needed to screen (NNS) is the number of individuals who must be screened to diagnose one case of TB. Operational research, in the context of TB, involves applied studies aimed at generating evidence to support the effective and sustainable implementation of interventions within health systems to improve health outcomes. The GRADE framework is widely used to summarize evidence and develop clinical and public health recommendations. Passive case-finding refers to the process where individuals with TB symptoms seek care on their own initiative, leading to diagnosis and treatment. In contrast, systematic screening involves actively identifying individuals at risk for TB disease within a target group using rapid assessments, tests, or examinations. Presumptive TB refers to individuals presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of TB. Previously treated individuals are those who have received at least one month of TB treatment in the past. Programmatic management of TB preventive treatment involves coordinated efforts to scale up preventive treatment for those at risk of developing TB. Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) is caused by strains resistant to rifampicin, and cases of MDR-TB and RR-TB are often grouped together for treatment purposes. Serious adverse events related to TB treatment include life-threatening conditions, hospitalization, or significant disability, and may require discontinuation of the suspected medication. Severe extrapulmonary TB includes miliary TB or TB meningitis. In children under 15 years, extrapulmonary forms of TB other than lymphadenopathy are considered severe. Following the WHO consultation in 2021, intrathoracic lymph node TB in children is now classified as pulmonary TB. TB is a preventable and curable disease, yet it continues to affect millions of children and adolescents worldwide. Children under 15 years account for approximately 11% of global TB cases, with one million children falling ill with TB annually. However, less than half of these cases are diagnosed or reported, with the largest detection gap in children under five years. Challenges in diagnosing TB in young children include difficulties in specimen collection and the paucibacillary nature of the disease, which limits bacteriological confirmation. Additionally, access to sensitive point-of-care diagnostic tests is limited. Adolescents, particularly those aged 15–19 years, are also significantly affected by TB, with an estimated 500,000 cases globally each year. Unlike young children, adolescents are a key group for TB transmission due to the infectious nature of their disease and their high social mobility. The WHO operational handbook on TB management in children and adolescents provides practical guidance for implementing evidence-based recommendations. It aims to reduce the burden of TB morbidity and mortality in children and adolescents, aligning with global targets such as the WHO End TB Strategy and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Contact investigation is a systematic process to identify individuals, including children and adolescents, with undiagnosed TB disease or infection among the contacts of a TB patient. This process often involves household or close contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB. Systematic screening for TB disease aims to detect cases early, minimize delays in treatment, and reduce transmission within the community. The operational handbook emphasizes the importance of childand adolescent-friendly healthcare services and provides guidance on TB screening, prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. It also addresses special situations, such as TB in children living with HIV, TB during pregnancy, and TB in malnourished children. The annexes include practical tools, resources, and standard operating procedures to support healthcare providers in managing TB in children and adolescents effectively.
